definition.text: How a country's total income, or GDP, is shared among its population.

facts.text: Classical economists such as Smith, Malthus and Ricardo studied factor income distribution, while modern economists focus on distribution across individuals and households.
Inequality is distinct from poverty and fairness; the Gini coefficient measures it from 0 (perfect equality) to 1 (perfect inequality), and the Lorenz curve can depict it.
In neoclassical theory, national income is distributed according to factor prices, the payment to each factor of production.
Policies that shape it include progressive taxation and public spending on education, healthcare and social security for lower-income groups.

The Kuznets curve holds that inequality rises as a country develops and falls once average income reaches a certain level, though many prominent economists disagree that rising inequality is necessary.
Income mobility, how people move in the earnings hierarchy over their lifetime, is measured by the association between parents' and adult children's socioeconomic standing.
Unionization reduces wage inequality; for American male workers the reduction was 1.7 percent in the private sector and 16.2 percent in the public sector.

title: Progressive tax

definition.text: A tax whose rate rises as the taxable amount rises, so a taxpayer's average rate is lower than the marginal rate.

facts.text: It shifts the incidence of tax toward those with a higher ability to pay; its opposite is a regressive tax, such as a sales tax, where the poor pay a larger share of income.
The marginal rate applies to each extra unit of income; the effective marginal rate also counts the loss of welfare benefits and tax credits.
Failure to index brackets to inflation causes bracket creep and fiscal drag, an effective tax increase.
Progressive taxation directly reduces income inequality, especially when it funds transfers and safety nets, though the effect may be muted if higher rates increase evasion.
The effect on growth is disputed: a 2008 OECD report found a weak negative relationship, while the IMF says some advanced economies could raise progressivity without hampering growth.
Hayek and Nozick opposed it on principle, arguing that it biases against wealth and weakens incentives, or that taxing labor earnings resembles forced labor.

contested_note: Economists and politicians debate whether progressive taxation helps or hinders growth and how far it reduces inequality.

definition.text: A system in which tax flows are inverted for incomes below a threshold, so low earners receive payments while those above pay tax.

facts.text: It is most commonly attributed to Milton Friedman and is offered as a less bureaucratic alternative to progressive tax systems.
Because subsidies adjust smoothly for poor households, it avoids the welfare trap faced by means testing.
